  • Appendix A: Changelog
    • Unreleased
    • webcpp 0.1.0

webcpp::beast is a C++20 compatibility facade for Boost.Beast applications. It preserves Boost.Beast’s messages, buffers and parsers while selecting a transport appropriate to the program’s environment. Native and WASIp3 socket programs use the guest protocol engine. Browser clients use WebSocket and fetch; WASI host HTTP programs use the host’s request and response resources. The application matrix distinguishes direct source compatibility from explicit counterparts, since a browser client and a host HTTP handler do not own a TCP listener.

Tutorial: construct a response

Use the library at libs/beast in the WebCPP superproject, with Boost 1.92 and B2 configured. This first example handles an in-memory request; it opens no connection.

http::response<http::string_body> handle_request(const http::request<http::string_body>& request) {
    http::response<http::string_body> response{http::status::ok, request.version()};
    response.set(http::field::content_type, "text/plain");
    response.body() = "Hello from WebCPP\n";
    response.prepare_payload();
    return response;
}

int main() {
    const http::request<http::string_body> request{http::verb::get, "/hello", 11};
    const auto response = handle_request(request);
    std::cout << response.result_int() << ' ' << response.reason() << '\n';
    std::cout << response[http::field::content_type] << '\n';
    std::cout << response.body();
}

From the superproject root, run:

unset CPATH CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH C_INCLUDE_PATH
b2 -a libs/beast/example//http_message.output

The expected output is captured from the same example compiled against upstream Beast:

200 OK
text/plain
Hello from WebCPP

The successful finish is a matched .output target. Compiling the executable alone does not check its result.

Exchange a message in the browser

Configure Emscripten and the project’s pinned Chrome. The browser driver serves controlled local peers and the compiled page, runs JSPI and Asyncify, and checks the page’s result. It does not substitute Node for the browser.

b2 -a toolset=emscripten variant=release libs/beast/example/browser//browser

The example resolves the local test peer and records its authority. These operations then exchange a text message through the browser’s WebSocket:

beast::websocket::stream<beast::tcp_stream> socket(io);
beast::get_lowest_layer(socket).connect(addresses, ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}
// These synchronous operations suspend into the browser event loop.
socket.handshake(host, "/echo", ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}
socket.text(true);
socket.write(boost::asio::buffer("hello", 5), ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}
beast::flat_buffer incoming;
socket.read(incoming, ec);
if (ec || beast::buffers_to_string(incoming.data()) != "hello") {
    return 1;
}
socket.close(beast::websocket::close_code::normal, ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}

The synchronous interface suspends the C++ stack while the browser handles the operation. Use the Asio suspension configuration supplied by the B2 dependency; blocking the browser thread would prevent the event that completes the wait.

The same example sends an HTTP message through fetch and validates the response:

beast::tcp_stream stream(io);
stream.connect(addresses, ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}
beast::http::request<beast::http::string_body> request{beast::http::verb::post, "/http", 11};
request.set(beast::http::field::host, host);
request.body() = "hello";
request.prepare_payload();
beast::http::write(stream, request, ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}
beast::http::response<beast::http::string_body> response;
incoming.consume(incoming.size());
beast::http::read(stream, incoming, response, ec);
if (ec || response.result_int() != 200 || response.body() != "hello") {
    return 1;
}
stream.socket().shutdown(net::ip::tcp::socket::shutdown_both, ec);
if (ec) {
    return 1;
}

A successful page prints browser tutorial: ok; the driver requires that result for both suspension variants. The controlled peer uses loopback HTTP. Production HTTPS/WSS connections use the browser’s certificate validation and trust store.

Handle a host HTTP request

The WASI example receives an HTTP request from the host and returns a Beast response. The host owns the listener, connection and any HTTPS termination:

// Copyright (c) 2026 WebCpp.org
//
// Distributed under the Boost Software License, Version 1.0. (See
// accompanying file LICENSE_1_0.txt or copy at
// https://www.boost.org/LICENSE_1_0.txt)

#include <webcpp/beast/wasi/http.hpp>

namespace http = webcpp::beast::http;

namespace {
/** Application routing and response construction, independent of listener ownership. */
http::response<http::string_body> handle_request(http::request<http::string_body> request) {
    http::response<http::string_body> response{http::status::ok, request.version()};
    response.set(http::field::content_type, "text/plain");
    if (request.target() == "/health") {
        response.body() = "ready\n";
    } else {
        response.body() = request.body();
    }
    response.prepare_payload();
    return response;
}
}  // namespace

// The host owns the listener and any HTTPS trust policy.
WEBCPP_BEAST_WASI_HTTP_EXPORT(handle_request)
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip2 variant=release libs/beast/example/wasi//http
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 variant=release libs/beast/example/wasi//http

The served test checks the health response and echoed request body against the example’s recorded request transcript. A failed response, timeout or mismatch fails the test. Supplying a guest TCP acceptor is unnecessary for this backend.

How-to: select a dependency and target

B2 dependency Purpose

/webcpp/beast//beast

Portable buffers, HTTP messages, parsers and serializers.

/webcpp/beast//sockets

Native/WASIp3 guest socket algorithms and Asio configuration.

/webcpp/beast//tls

Guest-owned TLS with source-built OpenSSL.

/webcpp/beast//browser

Browser-owned WebSocket, fetch and TLS policy.

/webcpp/beast//wasi-http

WASIp2/P3 host HTTP resources, without guest sockets or OpenSSL.

/webcpp/beast//wasi-streams

Explicit supplied-stream counterparts, including WASI CLI input/output.

Include <webcpp/beast/http/read.hpp> and <webcpp/beast/http/write.hpp> explicitly for byte-stream operations, and <webcpp/beast/tcp_stream.hpp> or <webcpp/beast/websocket.hpp> for the socket types. The convenience header omits these transport headers and <webcpp/beast/ssl.hpp>.

Select the dependency for the transport the application actually uses. A WASI host HTTP handler does not need the guest socket or TLS dependency. Combining backends is explicit, for example a WASIp3 service that accepts host HTTP requests and separately contacts a TCP service.

b2 -a variant=release exception-handling=on,off libs/beast/test libs/beast/example
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip2 testing.launcher=wasmtime exception-handling=on,off libs/beast/test libs/beast/example
b2 -a toolset=clang-wasip3 testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh exception-handling=on,off libs/beast/test libs/beast/example
b2 -a toolset=emscripten exception-handling=on,off libs/beast/test libs/beast/example

WASIp3 socket tests require the launcher’s loopback networking capabilities. Production hosts should grant only the capabilities their application needs.

Configure error policy

webcpp-beast-unsupported=error is the default; ignore is the alternative intended for documented host-adapter restrictions. It does not make an unavailable transport work. The B2 feature defines exactly one of WEBCPP_BEAST_UNSUPPORTED_ERROR and WEBCPP_BEAST_UNSUPPORTED_IGNORE. Defining both fails compilation.

WEBCPP_BEAST_NO_EXCEPTIONS follows <webcpp/config.hpp> and can also be defined by the application. WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS applies to all WebCPP libraries. These macros do not change the compiler configuration or remove upstream Boost overloads; use exception-handling=off for a complete build without exception handling. Prefer upstream error-code overloads when recovery is required.

Explanation: separate messages from transport

Boost.Beast’s general headers include stream algorithms that reach Asio sockets. A message-only application does not need those dependencies, even though the Asio port now offers a WASIp2 socket reactor. This facade exposes data headers separately, retaining upstream type identity and parsing behaviour without a guest reactor.

The socket backend executes upstream Beast over the existing Asio port. Host adapters map operations to browser WebSocket/fetch and wasi:http, preserving application-visible messages with documented differences in connection ownership, headers, framing and TLS. A host HTTP handler does not imply a TCP acceptor.

For a server counterpart, keep the application’s HTTP request processing and replace its accept loop with the host handler entry. For a local-stream counterpart, explicitly supply the two stream directions; stdin and stdout do not provide Unix socket names, descriptor passing or peer credentials.

Browser security remains the browser’s: CORS, forbidden request headers, certificate validation, redirects and WebSocket control frames cannot be implemented as arbitrary raw-socket options. Host TLS never uses guest OpenSSL settings. Prefer explicit errors to silently claiming that the host accepted an unavailable setting.

The native/WASI WebSocket allocator constructor accepts the portable constructor syntax, but upstream Beast still controls its internal stream-state allocation. Associated completion-handler allocators retain upstream semantics. Data containers use their upstream allocator template parameters.

set_server_name configures SNI only. It copies a non-terminated string view into a bounded buffer and rejects empty, overlong or embedded-NUL hostnames. Certificate and hostname verification remain separate TLS settings. Guest OpenSSL settings must never be represented as changing browser or WASI host trust policy.

Browser settings and observable differences

This table describes the browser-owned WebSocket and fetch backends. It does not change native or WASIp3 guest socket semantics. ERROR rejects an unsupported setting with operation_not_supported when the dependent operation starts. IGNORE discards that setting; it does not add a missing browser capability or disable browser security. Configuration is part of the browser types’ namespace; translation units using different policies cannot exchange those types silently.

The browser-owned WebSocket’s websocket::request_type uses http::basic_fields<std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<char>>. Its handshake fields therefore use the stream’s memory resource, including long decorator values. Use that alias, or a generic callable, when declaring a request decorator rather than requiring Boost’s default field allocator. Native and WASIp3 socket streams retain the upstream request type. The explicit guest WebSocket adapter accepts typed WebCPP request and response decorators for client and server handshakes; it converts their fields when calling the upstream protocol implementation.

The test harness configures an ephemeral CA in a disposable full-Chrome profile. The protocol contract peer’s certificate covers localhost and 127.0.0.1; an untrusted profile rejects its WSS connection before the trusted contracts run. Application HTTPS fixtures use a separate localhost-only certificate to prove that a trusted certificate is still rejected for the wrong hostname. These fixture settings belong to the host harness and do not add guest TLS controls.

Setting or operation Outcome Meaning for the application

SNI and host_name_verification matching the URL authority

Accepted

The browser performs its own certificate and hostname validation.

verify_peer, default verification paths, tls_client and sslv23_client

Accepted

The browser chooses its enabled protocol versions and trust store.

Fixed TLS version, verify_none, arbitrary verification callback

Unsupported

The application cannot change browser TLS validation or negotiation.

Unsupported

Guest certificate material does not configure the browser’s TLS stack.

Unsupported

The browser connects and authenticates the URL authority.

WebSocket decorator’s Sec-WebSocket-Protocol

Accepted

Its values become the browser constructor’s subprotocol list.

Unsupported

The browser constructs the handshake headers.

expires_after, expires_at, expires_never, handshake timeout

Accepted

An expired operation returns beast::error::timeout and closes the connection.

Accepted

Idle timeout with keep-alive pings; explicit ping and pong

Unsupported

control_callback

Ignored under both policies

The browser controls compression and frame boundaries.

Close code 1000 or 3000 through 4999

Accepted

The reason uses Beast’s bounded UTF-8 reason string.

Other close codes, including 1001

Unsupported

Under IGNORE, the adapter closes with 1000 instead.

read_message_max

Enforced

An oversized message reports message_too_big and closes the connection.

queue_limits

Enforced

Queued receives and browser-buffered sends have separate bounds. Exceeding one closes the connection with receive_limit or send_limit.

HTTP Host equal to URL host or host:port

Accepted

The browser generates the corresponding Host field.

HTTP Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding

Message framing accepted

The adapter sends decoded body bytes; fetch chooses wire framing.

HTTP Connection and Keep-Alive

Ignored under both policies

Connection ownership and reuse belong to the browser.

HTTP User-Agent and browser-forbidden request headers

Unsupported

The browser may reject, replace or omit these headers.

HTTP methods or bodies fetch cannot send, including CONNECT

Unsupported

IGNORE cannot make the browser issue a forbidden request.

Redirected HTTP response

Policy dependent

ERROR reports operation_not_supported; IGNORE returns the final response. The redirect has already been followed by fetch when this is reported.

CORS rejection, mixed-content rejection or another fetch failure

browser_errc::fetch_failed

The browser does not reliably expose a more specific cause.

Browser socket facade’s shutdown, close and cancel

Facade lifecycle operations

These stop pending facade work; they do not expose a TCP descriptor.

A successful WebSocket write means the browser accepted the message, not that the peer received it. Partial writes are accumulated into one message, and their bytes count toward the send bound. A cancelled read leaves the next message available to a later read. Destruction aborts pending operations through posted completion and unregisters event callbacks before late events can reach them. Both queue bounds default to 4 MiB. The default maximum WebSocket message is 16 MiB; a smaller receive-queue bound still applies independently. The receive bound charges each retained payload and its message record, including empty messages. Partial reads release that charge only when the complete message is consumed and its storage is released. Container bookkeeping and allocator overhead are additional implementation costs; the bound is not a total heap quota.

The default HTTP path maps messages directly to fetch. Its response body limit defaults to 8 MiB. http::async_read_header and http::read_header accept response messages and complete when metadata is available, before the body is consumed; a subsequent full read consumes the body. The separate http_byte_stream compatibility adapter synthesizes HTTP/1.1 bytes for programs using Beast parsers, buffering the full fetch response before parsing. Fetch has already decoded the response body, so synthetic responses omit original Content-Encoding and Content-Length; responses with a body use chunked framing. HEAD, 204 and 304 responses have no synthetic body or chunk terminator. HEAD parser users retain skip(true). These representation differences do not imply byte-for-byte equality with the original wire response.

Cancellation of host-supplied streams

The WASIp2 WebSocket counterparts use Asio’s pollable-driven CLI adapter and retain asynchronous read/write operations. Their actual client/server exchanges pass with both exception profiles. The P2 Asio supplied-stream lane checks a pending read with open, empty input, timer cancellation, cancellation slots, stream destruction, deferred initiation and handler allocator/executor associations. Other supplied counterparts retain their explicit synchronous partial operations.

Supplied-stream cancellation is checked between host calls and while waiting on supported readiness operations. It cannot preempt a host import that blocks the calling thread. In the tested Wasmtime 50 CLI, WASIp2 stdout can block when its operating-system pipe fills even after check-write grants permission. A paused consumer must resume draining before that import returns and the component can observe cancellation. Keep the consumer draining or select a host/channel with nonblocking write behaviour when a strict cancellation deadline is required.

This is separate from a guest socket’s cancellation semantics. Standard input and output also do not acquire Unix socket addressing or peer credentials merely because they are exposed through file descriptors.

Verification and reproduction

The local evidence below was collected on macOS ARM64 on 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-03 with Boost 1.92, native Clang 21, wasi-sdk 34, Emscripten 6.0.11 and Wasmtime 50.0.1. Core and guest TLS runs use Release builds. Browser contract runs use Debug, and the standalone upstream oracle compiles with -O0; these are correctness checks, not performance or binary-size measurements. A local pass does not establish Windows or Linux coverage; the remote CI report supplies those independent results.

Suite Profiles exercised What passed

Portable core and socket facade

Native single/multi, exceptions on/off; WASIp2/P3 single, exceptions on/off; Emscripten single, exceptions on/off

Public-header compilation, upstream type identity, binary HTTP bodies, parser limits, error policy, constructor conversion and applicable socket/SNI exchanges.

Guest TLS protocol

Native single/multi, exceptions on/off; WASIp3 single, exceptions on/off; WASIp3 cooperative, exceptions off

Eight scenarios with TLS 1.2 and again with TLS 1.3 in each profile: 112 scenario executions. HTTP and binary WebSocket transfer, normal close, wrong hostname, untrusted CA, cancelled body read, truncated TLS shutdown, cancelled shutdown and handshake timeout.

Browser and Node contract, plus browser tutorial

JSPI/Asyncify, exceptions on/off, ERROR/IGNORE

Real Chrome and Node 26 WebSocket/fetch exchanges, queue and body limits, timeout, cancellation, destruction, allocator alignment, reconnection and response reuse. Direct header reads complete while the server still withholds the body. The allocation counter distinguishes stream, handler and context resources and requires zero escaped global allocations and zero retained blocks after cleanup.

WASI host HTTP and supplied streams

WASIp2/P3 single, exceptions on/off; applicable WASIp3 cooperative tests

Bounded 256 KiB exchanges, request/response trailers, malformed requests, resource cleanup, cancellation and explicit CLI stream counterparts.

WASI host HTTPS

WASIp2/P3 single, exceptions on/off; WASIp3 cooperative, exceptions off

Six application counterparts and the shared sync/async body-and-trailer contract: 35 driver executions containing 125 TLS attempts. Trusted localhost succeeds; unknown CA and trusted wrong hostname fail. The documentation SSL client also proves mutual TLS and rejection without a client identity.

Upstream application inventory

Per-application and per-profile results below

All 53 executable definitions are cross-checked against upstream Jamfiles, CMake definitions and entry points. Source hashes protect the original corpus.

The TLS fixture synchronizes shutdown cancellation with the peer receiving close_notify; it does not rely on an arbitrary sleep or callback ordering. WebSocket close already tears down TLS and TCP, so its test verifies that result without starting a second TLS shutdown. Each protocol scenario has an outer five-second deadline, and the driver also bounds the whole process.

Guest-socket applications compile their Wasm component once with Wasmtime before the execution deadlines start. Compilation has a separate 60-second limit and records its command, duration and exit status. The driver runs only the artifact it produced in its private temporary directory, with matching engine features and epoch interruption enabled. Guest readiness retains its 15-second bound and protocol I/O retains its five-second bound. The WASIp3 driven-test envelope is 90 seconds: the compilation allowance plus the existing 30-second driver bound. Compilation failures report stdout and stderr without starting the guest.

The native WebSocket constructor regression checks same-type move and conversion from a concrete executor to any_io_executor, including deflateSupported=false. The configuration tests include a deliberately failing cross-translation-unit link with different browser policies and a matching-policy success control. An expected compile/link failure is a passing negative test only when B2 reports failed-as-expected and its success control also passes.

Reproduce a suite

Configure the project’s pinned SDKs and native Boost 1.92 in a B2 user config. Select Wasmtime 50.0.1 explicitly through PATH. Emscripten 6 requires Python 3.10 or newer; set EMSDK_PYTHON when the system’s default Python is older. The commands assume .local/user-config.jam and run from the superproject root. -a forces compilation and execution; separate build directories preserve logs and outputs across targets.

unset CPATH CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH C_INCLUDE_PATH
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam -a variant=release \
  exception-handling=on,off threading=single,multi \
  libs/beast/test libs/beast/example libs/beast/test/tls//tls
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam -a toolset=clang-wasip2 \
  variant=release exception-handling=on,off testing.launcher=wasmtime \
  libs/beast/test libs/beast/example libs/beast/test/wasi//http
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam -a toolset=clang-wasip3 \
  variant=release exception-handling=on,off \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/beast/test libs/beast/example libs/beast/test/tls//tls
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam -a toolset=clang-wasip3 \
  variant=release threading=multi exception-handling=off \
  testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh \
  libs/beast/test libs/beast/example libs/beast/test/tls//tls
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam \
  libs/beast/test/browser/peer//native_peer-program threading=multi
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam -a toolset=emscripten \
  variant=release exception-handling=on,off \
  libs/beast/test/browser//browser libs/beast/example/browser//browser

The native peer built above is shared by the browser and Node contract suites. Run the Node contracts separately:

b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam -a toolset=emscripten \
  exception-handling=on,off libs/beast/test/browser//browser-node

Repeat both contract commands with webcpp-beast-unsupported=ignore to exercise the second policy. The browser lane installs and runs pinned full Chrome. The Node lane executes the same Wasm programs in Node 26, using its WebSocket and fetch APIs; it does not replace the separate browser CORS and mixed-content checks. Host HTTP drivers start Wasmtime with a loopback listener and bounded request transcripts. Production network capabilities remain the embedding application’s responsibility.

HTTPS/WSS fixtures use temporary CAs. The protocol contract peer has a leaf valid for both localhost and 127.0.0.1, preserving its existing loopback request URLs. Its fresh untrusted Chrome profile must reject WSS with an authority error before the trusted contract exchange runs. The application fixture uses a separate leaf valid only for localhost; its trusted profile must reject that certificate when addressed as 127.0.0.1. Full Chrome receives each CA in a disposable profile, and Node receives the contract CA through NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS. The system trust store is unchanged, and neither fixture disables certificate verification. Production browser trust remains browser-owned.

The WASI HTTPS fixture embeds exactly Wasmtime 50.0.1 and supplies a private test root through its supported host hook. Rustls performs normal chain and hostname verification. This isolates the CA from the machine and avoids claiming that a guest OpenSSL test establishes host HTTPS behavior. The stock Wasmtime CLI uses its own public roots and does not expose a custom-CA command-line option.

cargo +1.97.1 build --locked \
  --manifest-path libs/beast/test/applications/host-tls/Cargo.toml \
  --target-dir .local/beast-host-tls
export WEBCPP_WASI_TLS_FIXTURE="$PWD/.local/beast-host-tls/debug/webcpp-beast-host-tls-fixture"
b2 --user-config=.local/user-config.jam \
  toolset=clang-wasip2,clang-wasip3 exception-handling=on,off \
  libs/beast/test/applications/host-tls//applications-host-tls

The 53 upstream applications and their adaptations have separate targets. Their matrix records compilation and execution separately, including unavailable programming models rather than selecting an empty fallback program. In particular, stackful Boost.Context coroutines, native threads and asynchronous DNS are not inferred from a successful C++20 coroutine or pre-resolved-address counterpart.

Application profile evidence

All 53 upstream executables remain in every profile. Each cell gives the compile/run result independently. P = measured pass, F = measured failure, B = blocked, U = unavailable, N = no measured result.

A passing counterpart preserves the measured application operations. It does not establish unchanged source, scheduling, DNS, TLS policy or failure semantics. Native oracle comparison covers payloads/status/modes, excluding fixture addresses and elapsed time. Local native measurements use macOS ARM64; other operating systems require their CI runs. Raw results and commands are retained by the drivers.

Adaptations and limits

  • WASIp3 uses a fixture resolver posting the known local endpoint. DNS worker threads remain unverified. Worker/system executors use an explicit event loop.

  • Host HTTP preserves file handlers or request/body operations. Host listeners, framing and TLS are distinct from guest sockets. Six HTTPS client counterparts run through a configured Wasmtime host with an isolated CA, rejecting unknown issuers and trusted certificates for the wrong hostname. The documentation client additionally measures host-owned mutual TLS and missing-identity rejection. The documentation server measures a host mutual-TLS frontend.

  • The host crawler retains upstream report aggregation and two asynchronous workers over bounded authority/path inputs. Its fixture uses two peers, six paths, four response statuses, and a truncated-response failure followed by continued work. Host HTTP combines transport phases: failures count as Read; separate DNS/connect/write/timer phase counts are unmeasured.

  • Supplied streams replace Unix-domain addressing with caller-provided stdio. P2 WebSocket counterparts retain asynchronous partial operations through Asio pollables; the other supplied counterparts use synchronous partial operations.

  • Browser fetch/WebSocket own DNS, framing and TLS. Guest CA lists, protocol pinning and handshake User-Agent are removed explicitly. HTTPS fixtures install an ephemeral CA in an isolated Chrome profile. A fresh untrusted profile rejects the certificate; the trusted profile rejects its incorrect IP hostname. No certificate-error bypass or system trust-store modification is used.

  • Exception-off counterparts retain error-code paths and successful operations; formerly throwing paths report failure and abort. Stackful Context remains blocked.

  • Asio P2 provides sockets and guest TLS, but the Beast guest-socket and guest-TLS application corpus still needs P2 integration and validation. Browser listeners and WASI Unix-domain socket addressing remain unavailable. WASIp3 cooperative EH-on lacks the toolchain exception runtime.

Reproduction

python3 libs/beast/test/applications/inventory.py --check
python3 libs/beast/example/applications/tools/prepare.py --clang-format clang-format
b2 libs/beast/test/applications//applications
b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 libs/beast/test/applications/wasip3//applications-p3
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/beast/test/applications/browser//applications-browser
b2 toolset=clang-wasip2 libs/beast/test/applications/host//applications-host
b2 toolset=clang-wasip2 libs/beast/test/applications/host-clients//applications-host-clients
cargo build --locked --manifest-path libs/beast/test/applications/host-tls/Cargo.toml --target-dir .local/host-tls
export PATH="$PWD/.local/host-tls/debug:$PATH"
b2 toolset=clang-wasip2 libs/beast/test/applications/host-tls//applications-host-tls
b2 libs/beast/test/applications/noexcept//applications-noexcept
b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 libs/beast/test/applications/noexcept//applications-single-noexcept
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/beast/test/applications/browser-noexcept//applications-browser
b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 libs/beast/test/applications/streams//applications-streams
b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 libs/beast/test/applications/streams//applications-websocket-streams
b2 libs/beast/test/applications/chat//applications-chat

Configure pinned toolchains with the standard B2 user configuration. Clear CPATH/C_INCLUDE_PATH/CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH. Runtime peers bind loopback ports, wait for readiness, enforce deadlines, and reap every process.

Guarantees and evidence

  • message_test.cpp checks upstream type identity, embedded-NUL payloads, parser body limits and malformed fields on every declared data target.

  • socket_test.cpp exchanges real HTTP and binary WebSocket payloads, completes both sides of a close handshake, and verifies a stalled peer reaches the stream timeout. Each case has a five-second outer deadline.

  • ssl_test.cpp checks SNI copying and rejection without replacing an existing valid name. It does not claim that an SNI setting authenticates the peer.

  • config_test.cpp checks compiler/global/library exception configuration, both unsupported-operation policies and rejection of conflicting definitions.

  • test/tls/protocol.cpp checks actual TLS HTTP and WebSocket exchanges, authentication failures, transfer cancellation and TLS shutdown outcomes.

  • test/browser/browser_test.cpp runs the browser contracts in Chrome. Its local server controls delayed headers and bodies, redirects, WebSocket closure and CORS.

  • test/applications/inventory.py verifies all 53 pinned upstream executables and their source hashes; application drivers compare explicit local exchanges.

http_byte_stream

Explicit synthetic HTTP/1.1 adapter for upstream parser and serializer algorithms.

webcpp::beast::browser::http_byte_stream

Explicit synthetic HTTP/1.1 adapter for upstream parser and serializer algorithms.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/browser/http_byte_stream.hpp>

template</* implementation-defined */ NextLayer>
class http_byte_stream;

Description

Fetch owns real framing. This adapter decodes an outgoing serialized request and exposes a synthetic chunked response. HEAD, 204 and 304 have no body framing. The adapter and its next layer must outlive every outstanding operation.

webcpp::beast::http::async_read

Receives the complete decoded fetch response into a Beast message.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/browser/http.hpp>

template<
    /* implementation-defined */ Stream,
    class Buffer,
    class Body,
    class Allocator,
    class Token>
auto
async_read(
    Stream& stream,
    Buffer&,
    boost::beast::http::response<Body, boost::beast::http::basic_fields<Allocator>>& response,
    Token&& token);

Description

The completion is posted through the associated executor and allocator. The completion signature is void(error_code, std::size_t). Fetch decoding precedes message delivery, and wire framing headers are normalized. The authority record response_body_limit bounds the decoded body before allocation.

Return Value

The result determined by the completion token.

Template Parameters

Name Description

Stream

Browser authority record or TLS-intent stream.

Buffer

Dynamic buffer type retained for Beast call compatibility.

Body

Beast body model used to encode or receive the message body.

Allocator

Allocator used by the HTTP message fields.

Token

Asio completion token selecting the asynchronous result type.

Parameters

Name Description

stream

Browser stream whose recorded authority selects the host operation.

response

Destination message, kept alive until asynchronous completion when applicable.

token

Completion token controlling handler construction and the return type.

webcpp::beast::http::async_read_header

Receives response metadata before fetch has consumed its body.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/browser/http.hpp>

template<
    /* implementation-defined */ Stream,
    class Buffer,
    class Body,
    class Allocator,
    class Token>
auto
async_read_header(
    Stream& stream,
    Buffer&,
    boost::beast::http::response<Body, boost::beast::http::basic_fields<Allocator>>& response,
    Token&& token);

Description

The next complete read consumes the retained response body; a metadata read leaves it untouched. The buffer parameter is retained for Beast call compatibility and receives no wire bytes.

The result determined by the completion token.

webcpp::beast::wasi::client::perform

Performs a suspending exchange, preserving the caller’s Beast body and field allocators.

Declared in <webcpp/beast/wasi/http.hpp>

template<
    class RequestBody,
    class RequestFields,
    class ResponseBody,
    class ResponseFields,
    class Trailers = boost::beast::http::fields>
std::size_t
perform(
    http::request<RequestBody, RequestFields>& request,
    http::response<ResponseBody, ResponseFields>& response,

    webcpp::wasi::http::transfer_options const& options = transfer_options(),

webcpp::beast::wasi::http_context

Drives bounded host readiness operations without a socket reactor or worker thread.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/wasi/async.hpp>

class http_context;

Description

poll performs one bounded scan and never waits for data. run yields the current component task between scans. Callers keep messages and resources alive until their completion handler runs. Posted completion storage is released before invoking the handler, so its associated allocator resource may be released there. Destroying the context abandons pending handlers and cancels their host resource operations before releasing state.

Name Description

executor_type

webcpp::beast::wasi::stdio_stream

stdin/stdout or a supplied descriptor pair, borrowed exclusively for this object’s lifetime.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/wasi/stream.hpp>

class stdio_stream;

Description

Descriptors are set nonblocking and restored on destruction, never closed. stdout is protocol-only; diagnostics belong on stderr. Readiness and cancellation are checked every ten milliseconds while blocked. This does not provide Unix-domain socket semantics.

webcpp::beast::wasi::supplied_stream

A borrowed pair of nonblocking host channels.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/wasi/stream.hpp>

class supplied_stream;

Description

A zero-byte successful read means EOF. A write of zero bytes means would-block. Providers report would_block when unready and wait handles readiness, deadline and cancellation. The adapter never buffers more than the caller supplies, never closes a channel, and promises no path addressing, socket options or peer credentials.

webcpp::beast::websocket::stream::async_read

Receives one complete WebSocket message into a dynamic buffer.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/browser/websocket.hpp>

template<
    class DynamicBuffer,
    class Token>
auto
async_read(
    DynamicBuffer& buffer,
    Token&& token);

Description

The completion is posted through the associated executor and allocator. The completion signature is void(error_code, std::size_t). Cancellation leaves queued messages available for a subsequent read. Only one read may be outstanding, and the destination must outlive completion.

Return Value

The result determined by the completion token.

Template Parameters

Name Description

DynamicBuffer

DynamicBuffer type receiving message bytes.

Token

Asio completion token selecting the asynchronous result type.

Parameters

Name Description

buffer

Dynamic buffer receiving message bytes and retained until completion.

token

Completion token controlling handler construction and the return type.

webcpp::beast::websocket::stream::async_write

Submits a complete message to the browser send queue.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/browser/websocket.hpp>

template<
    class Buffers,
    class Token>
auto
async_write(
    Buffers const& buffers,
    Token&& token);

Description

The completion is posted through the associated executor and allocator. The completion signature is void(error_code, std::size_t). Success means the browser accepted the bytes into its queue, not that the peer read them. Exceeding queue_limits::send closes the connection with browser_errc::send_limit.

Return Value

The result determined by the completion token.

Template Parameters

Name Description

Buffers

ConstBufferSequence providing request or message bytes.

Token

Asio completion token selecting the asynchronous result type.

Parameters

Name Description

buffers

Buffer sequence whose storage remains valid until completion.

token

Completion token controlling handler construction and the return type.

webcpp::beast::ssl_stream::async_handshake

Validates TLS intent and marks the authority secure without opening a TLS socket.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/browser/ssl_stream.hpp>

template<class Token>
auto
async_handshake(
    webcpp::asio::ssl::stream_base::handshake_type type,
    Token&& token);

Description

The completion is posted through the associated executor and allocator. The completion signature is void(error_code). The browser performs certificate validation when fetch or WebSocket opens the URL. Under ERROR, custom roots, credentials, version pins, callbacks, or mismatched names produce operation_not_supported; IGNORE leaves those choices to the browser.

Return Value

The result determined by the completion token.

Template Parameters

Name Description

Token

Asio completion token selecting the asynchronous result type.

Parameters

Name Description

type

Requested TLS role; only client is representable by browser host APIs.

token

Completion token controlling handler construction and the return type.

The browser rejected a URL or WebSocket subprotocol syntax.

The browser could not establish the WebSocket connection.

The outgoing WebSocket queue exceeded its configured bound.

WEBCPP_BEAST_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Records the facade’s exception policy for host-adapter implementations.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/beast/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_BEAST_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Description

Defined automatically when webcpp has no exceptions, or explicitly by the application. Host adapters report recoverable failures through error codes. Inherited upstream overloads and data types retain Boost’s own exception configuration.

Appendix A: Changelog

Changes to the unreleased Beast facade.

Unreleased

webcpp 0.1.0

  • Added portable HTTP data interfaces and native/WASIp3 socket operations.

  • Added optional guest TLS SNI configuration with hostname validation.

  • Added browser WebSocket and fetch adapters with explicit capability policies.

  • Added WASI host HTTP and supplied-stream application counterparts.

  • Fixed WebSocket executor conversion when per-message compression is disabled.

  • Fixed host completion storage lifetime and support for PMR operation allocators.

  • Fixed supplied-stream HTTP reads with small bounded buffers.

  • Added executable examples, API reference and a verified target matrix.
